title: Do Humans Represent a ‘Major Transition’ in Evolution?
content: We re-examine Maynard Smith and Szathmáry’s thesis that ‘human societies and language’ represent a major transition in evolution based on changes in the storage, transmission, and translation of information. We argue that they understated the scope and significance of the transition associated with humans, the most consequential effects of which lie in the translation of large quantities of non-genetic information to structure in the form of artificial creatures (automata) that mimic living organisms. Humans evolved three specialized anatomical features related to the storage, transmission, and translation of non-genetic information (enlarged brain, vocal tract, and hands) that function in concert to compute the solutions to problems of adaptation through an evolutionary computational process with non-genetic information. We treat artifact production sequences dating to 3.3–0.025 million years ago as algorithms and apply algorithmic information theory to measure the amount of information translated to structure (‘program size’). We find that the transition linked to humans is an extended and nonlinear process that may be subdivided into phases based on trends in artifact production program size and algorithmic complexity. The transition will be complete when self-reproducing automata begin to evolve independently of the organisms that generated them.
